Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National | Technology | Telecom Space Hubs Africa urges coordinated approach to make Ghana a key player in Africa’s space industry Source : Emmanuel Tetteh 16 November 2026 8:13pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
The Director of Space Hubs Africa, Kwaku Sumah, has called for a coordinated national approach to space science and technology, urging Ghana to move beyond discussions and translate its space ambitions into practical outcomes that benefit citizens.
He said the establishment of the proposed Ghana Space Agency presented an opportunity to organise the country's growing space ecosystem, bring stakeholders together and position Ghana as a major player in Africa's space industry.
Speaking on the sidelines of the 2026 Ghana Space Conference in Accra on Monday, November 16, Mr Sumah said this year's edition, themed From Vision to Action, was focused on identifying practical measures to ensure the agency meets the expectations and development needs of Ghanaians.
He noted that while last year's conference concentrated on defining Ghana's aspirations for the space sector, the focus had shifted to implementation following Cabinet approval for the formation of the Ghana Space Agency.
"This year, however, we've decided there's enough talking. It is time to take action," he said, adding that Ghana must seize the opportunity to establish itself as a key player in the African space industry.
The three-day conference, running from November 16 to 18, has brought together representatives from government ministries, Ghana's military services, scientists, technology professionals, entrepreneurs and students to discuss the country's space priorities.
Mr Sumah said the discussions were expected to produce an Accra Declaration 2026, capturing the needs and recommendations of different sectors to guide the proposed agency.
The document, he explained, would be presented to the Attorney-General's Office, the Office of the Presidency and relevant ministries to ensure the agency is established with the needs of the people and institutions at its core.
He identified inadequate coordination among individuals and organisations working in Ghana's space sector as one of the major challenges identified during the previous conference.
However, he said there had since been improvements, citing growing partnerships between the Ghana Space Science and Technology Institute (GSSTI), the National Disaster Management Organisation (NADMO) and the Ghana Navy.
He also welcomed increasing participation by students and other Ghanaians, stressing the need to sustain the momentum through stronger institutional and individual collaboration.
On the benefits of investing in space technology, Mr Sumah said satellite applications went beyond astronauts and space exploration, offering practical solutions to everyday challenges, including flooding, disaster management, communications and natural resource monitoring.
Using the recent Accra floods as an example, he explained that satellite technology could help authorities predict rainfall and identify vulnerable communities before disasters occur.
During flooding, satellite imagery could map affected areas, identify locations at risk and support evacuation planning, while post-disaster mapping could help assess damage and improve urban planning to prevent future occurrences.
He described satellite data as an important tool for improving decision-making across several sectors, including security, environmental management and natural resource protection.
Mr Sumah further highlighted three major applications of satellite technology: navigation, communication and Earth observation.
He explained that satellite navigation already supports everyday services such as Uber, Yango and Bolt by providing location and direction information to users.
Satellite communication, he said, could help extend connectivity over long distances and improve access to communication services in rural and underserved communities.
Earth observation, meanwhile, involves capturing images of the planet from space to monitor activities on the ground, track environmental changes and support disaster response.
He said the technology could provide detailed imagery, with resolutions of up to three metres, allowing authorities to monitor developments and make better-informed decisions.
Mr Sumah urged Ghanaians to recognise that satellite technology was already relevant to their daily lives and that the country needed a deliberate strategy to maximise its growing applications.
He said the industry would continue to evolve, making it important for Ghana to build local capacity, encourage innovation and ensure that citizens, particularly young people, had opportunities to participate.
"Space is for everyone. Satellite technology is for everyone," he said, calling for a coordinated effort among government, industry, academia and citizens to harness the technology for national development.
